clue.text: Sees clue reflecting tyre changes?

indicators.note: a reflection shows things the other way round, so the two words are read backwards together

parts.note: to see something is to spot it
a tip is a hint or clue

explanation.surface: A puzzled solver notices a clue apparently mirroring a mechanic changing tyres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflecting' reads both words backwards as one run; 'Sees' looks like the verb of the sentence but is a synonym to be swapped.
explanation.definitionFit: In motor racing, cars come into the pits mid-race chiefly to have their tyres swapped; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Burst his devious plot in the 17th century

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, the name of the plot rather than a synonym for plot

parts.note: to pop is to burst, as a balloon does

indicators.note: devious means winding or crooked, so the letters of his are twisted out of order

explanation.surface: Someone exposes a scheming man's underhand plan set in the 1600s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devious' is the anagram signal. The definition works by naming the famous plot: the answer is the word that goes before Plot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Popish Plot of 1678 was an invented Catholic conspiracy against Charles II, made up by Titus Oates.

clue.text: Overcome? If not, he could be a Shakespearean character

indicators.note: could be says these letters might, rearranged, become something else

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wry aside: if a man is not overcome, perhaps he is a figure out of Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges the letters of OVERCOME, IF NOT and HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello is styled the Moor of Venice in the play's full title, so the phrase names that tragic hero.

clue.text: Now Bill turns up in play

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the word for play

parts.note: to toy with something is to play with it

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning up reads the word from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a bill or poster

explanation.surface: A man called Bill suddenly appears in a theatre production at this moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is an advertisement; 'turns up' reverses it and 'in' sets it inside the word for play.
explanation.definitionFit: Today, as an adverb, means at the present time, in these days.

clue.text: Shakespearean lawyer from same place as 2 heard fast car

parts.words: Shakespearean lawyer from same place as 2
parts.note: Portia, disguised as a lawyer, defends Antonio in The Merchant of Venice; 2 is the Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: A sports car somehow linked to a Venetian heroine of Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, PORTIA sounds like the car maker's name, PORSCHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Porsche is a German maker of high-performance sports cars.

clue.text: Rain oddly masks King Jack?

indicators.note: oddly picks the odd-numbered letters, the first and third, of rain

parts.note: PPE, personal protective equipment, includes face masks
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Wet weather apparently covers up a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the odd letters of 'Rain' gives RI; then PPE, then R.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack the Ripper was the Victorian London murderer; the question mark admits the forename is only a clue to the surname.

clue.text: Celebrity team, cycling visionaries

a side is a sports team

explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves ALISTS from the front of ALISTSIDE to the back, leaving IDE + ALISTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Idealists pursue high principles and dreams of how things could be, as visionaries do.

clue.text: Shakespearean character has no defence (almost) for breaking into clothes shop

indicators.note: into says the scrambled letters go inside the shop's name

parts.note: Primark is a British chain of cheap clothes shops

almost drops the final letter of no defence

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare figure, left unguarded, breaks into a clothing store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the final letter, 'breaking' scrambles the rest and 'into' sets it inside PRIMARK, a British budget clothing chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark in the play's full title, so the phrase names that character.

clue.text: Notice concerning wild tigers

clue.text: They make cases for soft heads

heads are leaders, as of departments

clue.text: Compatriot of 7, explorer asleep when leaving run-down area

explanation.walkthrough: 7 is the Prince of Denmark, so a compatriot is a Dane.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitus Bering was a Danish-born navigator in Russian service who gave his name to the Bering Strait.

clue.text: Compatriot of 7, scientist starts to buy off his rivals

explanation.definitionFit: Snowy, Milou in French, is the white fox terrier who accompanies Tintin.

clue.text: Maybe Oliver's unwell companion enters the French stone monuments

explanation.definitionFit: A cromlech is a prehistoric megalithic tomb, a dolmen of upright stones topped by a capstone.

clue.text: Taps into Native American's nursery

clue.text: Part of poem about irritatingly late painter of 2's city

indicators.note: irritatingly suggests being stirred up, so the letters of late are jumbled

explanation.walkthrough: 'irritatingly' scrambles and 'about' wraps the poem section round. 2 is the Moor of Venice, so the city is Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Canaletto was the 18th-century Venetian painter famous for detailed views of Venice.

clue.text: Teacher served up only item on menu

clue.text: Lover of 2's city has about a month in South Africa

clue.text: Fools an ugly Spaniard

clue.text: In the end, to follow illegal rules is for the birds

clue.text: Next to live party

clue.text: As viruses are excellent, starts to live largely underground like angora rabbits

clue.text: Primates discommode parishioners — not all return

clue.text: It's used to assemble friend broken knee hampers
